response_text:
Honestly, I think YTA (you’re the asshole) for not cutting the customer’s hair, even though I understand you didn’t mean any harm and you were trying to follow your shop’s policies and respect your employees.

Here’s the situation: You run a barbershop where about 99% of the customers are men. Occasionally, women are served, but only by appointment with your one female hairstylist, as clearly stated on your shop’s signage, Facebook, and website. Your staff is mostly male and Muslim, and for religious reasons, your male staff can’t touch women’s hair unless they’re family. You don’t train your team for women’s haircuts – pretty understandable since the techniques, products, and tools can be really different.

But here’s the sticky part – the customer in question was a male-presenting woman wanting a men’s style haircut. Even though the price would be the same, and even though it was a "men’s" haircut, you stuck to your women-by-appointment policy and didn’t let anyone cut her hair. She was told to come back another time when the female stylist could be called in, but that would have required hours of advance notice. You say you felt bad, but overall chose to uphold staff religious requests and keep your standards.

I'm all for respecting religious beliefs and honesty about skill sets (no sense in messing up a haircut because you aren't actually trained for it), but at the end of the day this was an awkward and unwelcoming experience for a paying customer just because of her gender—regardless of how she presented herself or the type of haircut she wanted. The fact that women do get served at your shop shows it can be done, so the policy is flexible when convenient. If you want to stick to men's hair only, that would be more straightforward, but as is, it was kind of gatekeeping. If you’re going to say yes to serving men and “by appointment only” women, you need to consider nonbinary or trans people (who often don’t fit cleanly into these gendered policies) and update your policy to be more fair to everyone, or at least, train your staff to handle these situations with care and compassion.

You weren’t being malicious, but YTA for sticking to a gendered policy rigidly and not finding a way to help, especially since a simple men’s haircut was all she asked for. Sometimes rules need rethinking, especially when they unintentionally exclude people.

Honestly, I don’t think you’re in the wrong here at all (so, no, you’re NTA). You manage a barbershop that’s super clear about its policies – both in-person and online – stating that women are served by appointment only due to your staff’s religious practice, the difference in hair techniques, and the fact you have just one female stylist for these services. Your staff, who are primarily Muslim men, have a religious rule about not touching women’s hair unless she is family, and the necessary tools and training for women’s haircuts aren’t even part of the shop’s daily operations.

You did your best – the price would have been the same, but you just asked for a couple of hours’ notice so the only female barber could come in for the appointment. The signage, your Facebook, and your website make all this totally transparent. The fact that your clientele is about 99% men, but you still provide an option for women (even if appointment-based), shows you’re not trying to turn anyone away, just being respectful of your staff’s beliefs while still offering the needed service.

It’s understandable to feel bad for the customer, especially since they presented as a male-passing woman wanting a men’s haircut – but at the end of the day, you have to honor your employees’ boundaries and maintain a business flow where quality and respect for personal/religious practice come first. Refusing the walk-in, under clearly established policy, doesn’t make you the bad guy here. You’re simply making sure your shop is run properly and respectfully for both clients and staff.

Honestly, I think YTA in this situation. Here's why: It sounds like your barbershop mostly serves men (99% of clientele), but you *do* sometimes serve women by appointment—this is clearly posted on your signage, on Facebook, and your website. I get that your staff are mainly Muslim, and that male staff aren’t comfortable cutting women’s hair due to religious reasons, AND that they’re not trained for women’s cuts. But in this case, the customer was a male-passing woman just looking for a men’s style cut—something your team gives all the time.

It seems like the only issue was she hadn’t booked in advance, but your policy doesn’t appear to ban walk-in women, just suggests appointment required. Still, did you at least try to compromise, or make her feel welcome for returning with an appointment?

Her experience—being turned away when asking for a standard haircut, and then labeled as the problem—is understandably upsetting, especially if your handling (even unintentionally) came off as policing gender. Even if you stick to your religious and training policies, there can be a better way to handle this that doesn’t leave someone feeling discriminated against. The fact that you apologized and offered the same price doesn’t change that in-the-moment rejection stings, and your business practices DO impact people—especially gender nonconforming folks.

So yes, I think you were wrong here, AITA. There’s room for both your policies and for empathy/clarity in communication so no one leaves feeling bullied or excluded.

Absolutely **NTA** (Not The Asshole) here. Let me break down why, given all the facts:

- This barbershop is managed specifically with a 99% male clientele and that’s reflected in *everywhere*: the men-focused décor, skill training, and tools—which are different from what you need to cut women’s hair!
- There is a clear, posted women-by-appointment policy—highly visible on the shop’s signage, Facebook, AND official website—so it’s definitely not hidden or discriminatory. Anyone can see ahead of time that appointments for women require some notice.
- All the staff are primarily Muslim, and some men there follow their *religious* practice of not cutting women’s hair unless they're immediate family. That’s a major aspect of respecting their beliefs, not just a random shop rule.
- On top of the religious aspect, the shop staff are straightforward: they’re not trained for women’s hair, and working on it requires different techniques and products—so they’d call in a *female stylist* in these situations.
- In the situation that happened, a customer the manager described as a male-passing woman came in and wanted a men’s style cut, with expectation of walk-in service. Still, because of their policy and the men's discomfort (religious reasons), no available barber would serve her right away—but the manager specifically said pricing would be fair (just like telling *anyone* about cost—no gender discrepancy) and explained they needed a couple hours’ notice to call the right stylist in.
- Instead of booking, the customer sadly accused the staff of bullying, transphobia, and sexism, and left upset.

Personally, I think as long as the business is totally upfront about its policies and accommodates all genders via appointment, there shouldn’t be blame here. The refusal wasn’t because of *who* she was, it was about respecting staff beliefs and their training limitations. Plus, a clear option was offered! It’s totally fair to ask for notice if specific skills, staff and sensitivities are involved.

No one was *targeted*—just respectful boundaries, well-advertised, and a legitimate request for extra time that would apply *to any woman*, regardless of how she looks or what style she wants.

Bottom line: manager’s not at fault. If you've set policies around clear, reasonable concerns (skill, staffing, religious practice) and offer another equitable option instead of outright refusing, that's not discrimination. It's actually just being a good, considerate business.

Okay, I understand why someone might be upset in that situation, but honestly—I think YTA (yes, you're the asshole) for refusing to cut the customer’s hair without trying harder to explain or accommodate. 

Here’s why: Your shop *does* have a boundary in place—a clear women-by-appointment policy. I’ll give some points for transparency here, since you Mention on your signage, Facebook, and website that women have to book in advance. I also totally understand that most of your staff and barbers are Muslim, and those who are male follow religious rules not to cut women's hair unless it's family, which is culturally and personally important.

You've also made it clear that the shop doesn’t train in women's hair due to different techniques, products, and your religious practice. You have a female stylist who comes in by appointment just for women's haircuts. The rule seems consistent: because no one on duty felt comfortable, the female barber wasn't there and couldn't come in at the drop of a hat.

But where you went wrong, in my opinion, was not making things flexible—if the customer was already in the shop and this policy wasn’t explained before they arrived, it would absolutely suck to be turned away, especially if they're just looking for a haircut and you tell them “wait a couple of hours.” Even if you did explain beforehand, people often miss online details, and refusing without empathy leaves a bad vibe, whether or not accusations of transphobia or sexism are *personally* fair in this very context.

So yes—you’re technically in the right religiously, ethically according to your rules, and by your shop policy, but if you’re running a business that’s open to the public, you need to have really clear signage, great customer service, and do more to make people feel welcome, even if you can’t serve them immediately. Otherwise, you look unsympathetic at best and prejudiced at worst. 

Bottom line: Treat people kindly and proactively resolve conflict—otherwise, YTA, even with a policy and religious justification.

Honestly, I don’t think you’re in the wrong here at all. The shop has a clearly posted women-by-appointment policy that’s shown on signage, Facebook, and the website—it’s really clear and transparent. There’s a female barber/hairstylist who handles women’s cuts, specifically by appointment, because the staff is mostly Muslim men who follow a religious rule not to touch women’s hair unless they’re family. That’s a valid religious boundary, and the shop designed their policy around it.

Also, the shop doesn't train the staff to work on women’s hair, both because of the religious practices AND the fact that women’s hair uses totally different techniques, products, and even tools. You gave the customer the option of calling in the female stylist, and told them the price wouldn’t change, there just needed to be a couple hours’ notice to get her in for an appointment.

It really sucks that the customer accused you of transphobia, sexism, and bullying, but that honestly isn’t what happened here. It was about respecting both the religious rules of the staff *and* the practical differences in training. No one refused to serve them out of hate or discrimination—it was a logistical thing and all fully disclosed by policy. You stuck to the rules which are there for everyone’s comfort and safety.  So no, you’re not the asshole for not cutting that customer’s hair.

Honestly, after reading all the facts, I have to say YTA (You're the Asshole) for not cutting the customer's hair. Yes, the shop has a clear women-by-appointment policy, and it's posted everywhere: on the signage, Facebook, and the website. I totally understand that the staff are primarily Muslim and have religious reasons for not touching women's hair unless they're family. I also get that your shop doesn't train the barbers in women's hair, since the techniques, products, and tools can be very different.

BUT, in this specific case, we're talking about a customer the manager described as a "male-passing woman" requesting a men's haircut—something you already know how to do. The shop wasn’t being asked for special products or complicated styling techniques, just a typical men’s style. And you said the price would've been the same—so basically, you treated the person like any male customer until you clarified their gender and then refused service because of shop policy.

I get that you need a female stylist for women, and you said you could have called her in with a couple hours’ notice, but honestly, if the hair being cut and the style requested are no different than what you cut for other men all day, this just feels like exclusion. It’s reasonable that the customer felt discriminated against—they even accused the staff of transphobia, sexism, and bullying, and honestly, it's not hard to see why with how the situation played out.

At the end of the day, policies shouldn’t override treating people respectfully and equally. Unless you genuinely couldn't give this customer a haircut because of demonstrated lack of skills or training (which doesn't seem the case here), this came off as needlessly rigid and, yes, a bit discriminatory. I think you should have made accommodations in the moment and been more flexible. Just doesn’t seem right that the customer got turned away for something you usually do.

Honestly, I don't think you're in the wrong here at all. The facts make it pretty clear: your barbershop has a clearly posted women-by-appointment policy—it's on your signage, Facebook, and website, so no one could reasonably say they weren't informed. The staff being mostly Muslim, with a genuine religious rule that prevents male barbers from cutting women's hair unless they're family, is a big deal. that's not just "preference," it's part of their faith.

On top of that, you don't train your staff for women's hair, both because it requires different techniques and tools and also due to your religious practices. When a customer, reportedly a male-passing woman, came in asking for a men's style haircut, your staff still stuck to policy—they didn't refuse on the basis of style or appearance, but because they need a women’s appointment so the right stylist, a woman in this case, could be called in. You even offered to do it for the same price if they'd wait for a couple hours! It's not like anyone was trying to overcharge or deny service based on identity.

It's sad that the customer accused you all of transphobia, sexism, and bullying but honestly, from what you've shared, the refusal was about upholding both your shop's policy and respecting the religious practices of your staff—not about discriminating. I get that from the customer's perspective this might've felt frustrating, but it's not unreasonable on your part. So no, you are NOT the asshole—religious boundaries and clear policies matter, and you even had an honest solution (female barber by appointment) that follows your shop’s ethical guidelines.

After reading everyone's perspectives, I'm definitely more aware of how impactful these kinds of policies can feel for people who don’t fit traditional expectations or might not see the fine print in advance—especially since just asking for a men’s haircut isn’t much different from what the barbers do all day. That said, my core view remains that the shop wasn't acting maliciously or in a discriminatory way on purpose: the women-by-appointment policy is extremely clear on all their platforms, the rationale (religious boundaries and actual training limitations) is valid, and there really was an offer to accommodate if the customer could wait for the appropriate staff. Still, I do see how, in the moment, it could come off as rigid or unintentionally exclusionary and how offering just a bit more flexibility, understanding, or even on-the-spot dialogue might have softened that blow. So, while I believe the refusal was rooted in reasonable boundaries, hearing from everyone makes me think the shop could improve in expressing empathy and perhaps update training or policies to account for those awkward in-between situations, like this one. Ultimately though, I still say **NTA** given the facts—but there’s room for growth in how inclusivity and customer care are handled.

Reading through the other perspectives has given me a lot to consider. The points made by those calling me NTA are strong: my barbershop’s policy is very explicit and visible, with the intent not to discriminate but to respect both religious beliefs and staff training/blind spots—it’s true that we thought ahead to allow a fair option for women via appointment with the right stylist. However, views 2, 4, and 6 bring up uncomfortable and valid arguments about how policies (even well-intentioned ones) can feel rigid or exclusionary in direct practice, especially for customers on the margin of expectations—like gender nonconforming or trans individuals. The recurring idea that if a customer requests a haircut I’m already trained for (in this case, a men’s cut on short hair), perhaps it calls for some individual flexibility, regardless of gender policy, rings true to me; my hardline rule may unintentionally create negative, even hurtful, experiences.

So, while I do continue to understand and value the reasons for the policy (religious, cultural, practical), I find myself less confident that my actions were wholly justified—context matters, and customer feelings in the moment can’t be discounted. I still think clear communication and being transparent about the "why" is crucial and helped, but I can see now how even following the posted rules can end up feeling unwelcoming. Maybe I wasn't necessarily malicious or intending discrimination, but I didn't do enough to bridge understanding or make the customer feel seen in their scenario; in practice, I could have been kinder or at least found a better way to help. Ultimately, my view lands somewhere in the middle: I acknowledge that neither intent nor policy fully excuses a negative experience, and I (reluctantly) still lean toward thinking I was the asshole in this case—even if not ethically wrong, I failed at real-world compassion. So, my updated stance—soft YTA for refusing to cut the customer’s hair without more flexible or empathic problem-solving, despite following policy.

After hearing everyone’s perspectives, I still lean toward YTA, but I now see more nuance. Several folks made strong points about the importance of respecting religious practices, the shop's clear policies being posted everywhere, and the real difference in technical skills for women’s vs. men’s hair—those are valid reasons for having the appointment policy with a female stylist. That does make the situation less clear-cut and suggests the refusal wasn't personal or overtly discriminatory. However, what keeps me at least partly in the "asshole" camp is that the rigidity of the shop’s policy didn’t leave room for empathy or flexibility, especially when a customer who genuinely appeared to just want a men’s haircut was left frustrated and feeling excluded. I get that rules are rules, but shops open to the public—especially in diverse areas—sometimes have to be ready to handle situations with kindness and understanding that policies don’t capture every scenario. So, while I have more understanding of your reasoning after seeing others defend it, I still believe this situation highlights the limits of strict policies and shows a need to update both customer handling and perhaps shop procedure, especially for people who don't fit easily into the categories the rules are built for. You weren't malicious, but the outcome was unwelcoming, so I think there's room—and a real need—for more consideration here.

Having read everyone else’s thoughts and revisited the situation, I appreciate the arguments people made about how turning away any customer seeking a standard men's haircut—especially a person presenting masculine and wanting a "men's cut" you already know how to do—can easily come off as exclusionary or needlessly rigid, particularly to those who feel vulnerable or marginalized. The point about adapting policies for nonbinary, trans, or gender-nonconforming folks also hits home, since a super-strict policy can cause people to feel unwelcome even if that wasn't anyone's intent. That said, I still believe that clear communication, respect for staff religious boundaries, and transparently posted policies (which *were* all in place here) are legitimately important factors. It wasn’t about denying service because of who the customer was, but rather about only providing the right service in a way that doesn’t put staff in a compromising position or require them to violate faith, plus considering limitations in skills (since the training focus is men’s cuts). Where I do see room for improvement, after reading these responses, is in finding more compassionate ways to explain the policy in-person—and perhaps considering how to better address edge cases when someone requests an entirely ordinary men's haircut regardless of their gender. So my view is that I'm still leaning toward "not the asshole" given the full transparency, fairness, and religious context, but I now think some aspects of your policy and communication with walk-ins—especially gender-nonconforming ones—could use thoughtful refinement to avoid people feeling dismissed or discriminated against.

After reading everyone else’s viewpoints and thinking again about the situation, I still feel conflicted but mostly stand by my initial opinion: YTA, but I better understand where those who disagreed are coming from. A lot of folks emphasized that your women-by-appointment policy is posted and crystal clear, the staff’s religious beliefs around not touching women’s hair are sincerely held, and that the differing haircut techniques further support the rule—those factors aren’t about targeting or discriminating against the customer personally. That said, what still bothers me is that the “policy” falls down in these very gray, real-life moments—this was a male-presenting woman, asking for a simple men’s cut (your most common service), not some advanced women’s specialty, and turning her away made the shop come off as needlessly rigid and insensitive to the awkward situation it put her in, especially when it could be seen as gatekeeping based strictly on perceived gender instead of haircut type. It’s clear nobody at the shop meant harm, but impact matters as much as intent—if policies like this continually alienate people on the margins (especially gender-nonconforming folks), it’s an ethical signal something might need to change, like trying gentle exceptions for common men’s services, or having staff trained on this for future accommodation. So while I more fully appreciate the logistics and faith reasoning behind the rule, I still ultimately think the customer was let down in this case; you could have handled it with more flexibility or warmth. I remain (if only slightly) with the opinion: YTA, but recognize why others feel you’re not.

After reading everyone’s perspectives, I can honestly see where those who say YTA are coming from, especially since from the customer’s side it likely felt exclusionary and that experience matters. I still stand by my view that the intent wasn’t mean-spirited or actively discriminatory—it really was about upholding a well-advertised policy rooted in staff comfort and religious boundaries, plus a genuine training limitation. However, I do see now that for someone presenting as male and wanting a typical men's haircut, the policy feels a bit rigid—if it only comes into play once gender is clarified, it can look like gender-policing, even if that’s not the intent. I still don’t think refusing the walk-in was unjustified given the posted policy, but I agree there’s definitely room for improvement in communicating empathy and possibly in how exceptions are handled when the staff feels truly able. Maybe the policy could use an update or training could be improved for these “grey area” moments so no one leaves feeling excluded. So overall, I still don’t think you’re the asshole by the letter of your business practice, but I better understand why the customer (and several here) felt the outcome wasn’t fair—and maybe a bit more flexibility or compassion could’ve made a difference.

After carefully reading through the additional perspectives, I still lean toward thinking YTA, though I do recognize a bit more nuance and see that this situation is certainly complicated. Several people argued that the policies were clearly posted and rooted in religious practices/training, and I appreciate that those boundaries matter — especially since refusing could be genuinely uncomfortable for your staff because of their faith. It's true the female stylist system is meant to respect everyone's comfort and that you offered her the same price and an option to wait, not an outright denial. But the reality remains: the customer received the same generic men's cut that male customers get daily, but she alone was told to come back, all based on assumed gender, even if that isn’t how you meant it. Regardless of what’s posted, it's very easy for anyone — especially someone GNC or trans — to feel singled out or shut out by gatekeeping, intentional or not. Yes, rules are clear and technically fair, but they do need to evolve if they're harming people who just need a basic, standard service. I respect the honesty and recognize you followed your shop's stated approach, but I still feel you could have accommodated the customer without violating staff beliefs—maybe by developing clearer staff training or adapting policies for edge cases like this. I acknowledge this isn't straightforward at all, and can see why people defend sticking to policy. Still, the impression left to the customer matters, especially in tense, identity-based moments like this. So, my position remains that you should have tried harder to make space for this person, even though I have more respect for the intent and context behind the shop’s approach after hearing all sides.

Reading through all the responses, I’m struck by how many people—while recognizing the clarity of the policy and the intent behind it—still really emphasize the customer’s experience and perception, especially since she was requesting a men’s haircut, something the shop routinely does for male clients. Some make fair points about how, regardless of intent, rigidly following gender-boundary policies can feel exclusionary, especially in cases involving nonbinary, trans, or gender-nonconforming individuals. That makes me pause, even though my initial instinct is to defend the policy (since it's well-posted, religion-based, and service for all women is by appointment). Still, reading these perspectives, I realize there’s room to improve how we present and handle these moments—perhaps through clearer, even warmer communication, and by explicitly flagging the men-only/training aspect before customers walk in, to lessen the chance for uncomfortable encounters. But ultimately, I still don’t think refusing the haircut in that situation—given religious staffing, training limitations, and having set up a straightforward, non-discriminatory path (female barber by notice)—makes the shop the “asshole.” However, I see how easily situations like this could be misread, and I now think that along with following the policy, more care and empathy in explaining it are truly needed. So, my general view stays the same (NTA), but I do now better appreciate why adapting policies and boosting communication could help avoid misunderstandings and hurt, especially for people who feel singled out by such gendered rules.

Having taken in all the additional opinions, I'm struck by the repeated emphasis many place on the customer’s personal experience—how being turned away, even gently, due to a rigid gender-based policy can still sting, especially when requesting a service routinely provided to others. At the same time, I continue to stand by my sense that the policy’s existence is neither arbitrary nor mean-spirited: it’s clearly posted, anchored in religious and professional boundaries, and an alternative was offered (wait for the female stylist), all steps taken to avoid outright exclusion. Yet, reading how others point out the ways strict adherence to such policies can inadvertently alienate trans, gender-nonconforming, or even just masculine-presenting women does sway me a little—especially since even fully transparent rules can feel like gatekeeping for those who don’t conform to expected categories. I now realize policy clarity isn’t always enough; the delivery and sensitivity matter a lot too. So, I maintain that, by the letter of how the shop runs and with what was offered, **not the asshole** still feels correct based on the information—there was no targeted rejection, and options existed—yet I see clearly that there’s significant room to grow in both communication style and perhaps smoothing the hard lines of such policies for edge cases so no one feels sidelined or embarrassed in the moment. My view’s softened: the action isn’t an AH move, but the process—and maybe the policy—could definitely show more human warmth to those caught outside the standard boxes.

After reflecting further on everyone’s newest rounds of input, my understanding has deepened—especially from those underscoring how even well-meaning, well-posted policies can feel unfair or exclusionary in those "gray area" moments, like turning away someone who just wanted a standard men’s haircut. I appreciate anew why protecting staff comfort and religious boundaries is important, and I still firmly believe our shop wasn’t being malicious or covertly discriminatory; the rules are explicit and present a pathway for all clients, and certain accommodations are based on staff ability, not pure gender policing. That said, patterns in these discussions convince me more than before that in practice, the strict enforcement of this policy—when staff can and does cut the requested hair type—risks alienating people for reasons that outweigh policy purity, especially for marginalized folks. I see no simple resolution: if we flex the rule, we may create staff discomfort; if we don’t, we can cause customers to feel rejected and unseen. But the consensus does tip me more toward accepting the criticism: intent matters, but so does the real impact, and purely following posting and procedure clearly wasn’t enough to make the customer feel welcome or respected. I still think religious context and transparency matter, and I wasn’t acting from malice, but I now more solidly land on “soft YTA”—these edge cases require not just rules, but compassion and adaptation, and I failed to really provide that in the moment. I think policy and staff training must be updated, or future customers will continue to feel unjustly turned away, no matter our intentions.

After reading through the new round of responses and thinking about the detailed reasons people provided, I still lean toward YTA, but I want to acknowledge the amount of nuance in this discussion that others have brought to light. It's clear that the barbershop’s policy—with women needing appointments for both religious and skill-based reasons—was not designed to be discriminatory, and I accept that the rules were both advertised and followed consistently. That said, what stands out from many perspectives (especially those emphasizing customer impact) is how the execution of this policy in real life—when applied rigidly—made at least this particular customer feel excluded, if not discriminated against. The example of someone simply wanting a standard men’s cut—a request that falls squarely within the shop’s day-to-day skills—demonstrates where policies can unintentionally miss the mark and leave certain people in uncomfortable positions. On the other hand, I do now see more clearly the challenge for staff asked to balance personal/religious comfort with customer service and the concern about setting a precedent by making exceptions. Ultimately, I can better recognize the reasoning and intentions beneath the refusal, but what remains for me is the importance of not just what the policy is, but the real-world impact it has. For that reason, while I don't think anyone here was purposefully being an "asshole," I still believe more flexibility, improved communication, and empathy are needed for edge cases like this—meaning I still lean to YTA, but mostly in the hope that it sparks genuinely needed change, not because the shop was malicious or unreasonable.

After more consideration and reading everyone's updated perspectives, I’m still leaning toward “not the asshole” (NTA) because of the genuinely clear policy, legitimate religious/training reasons, and good faith effort to accommodate through the by-appointment female stylist. But the repeated emphasis from others on the impact of these policies—especially how rigid enforcement can come across as exclusionary for people outside gender norms—really resonates after hearing everyone out. While I don’t think the refusal was malicious or based on personal bias, I now recognize more strongly that the practical effect was understandably hurtful to the customer. In hindsight, I see there’s space to handle such moments with added warmth and flexibility, or even to proactively discuss how staff might deal with “gray areas” where the haircut requested doesn’t match the gender expectations behind the posted rule. So while my bottom-line answer is still NTA because I followed policy and respected legitimate boundaries, I’m more convinced than before that there’s an ethical responsibility, as a business, to prevent even unintentional exclusion—perhaps by updating the approach to these scenarios, training on compassionate communication, and thinking creatively about genuine accommodation. In sum, listening has reinforced my view that intent and transparency matter, but so does minimizing any customer’s sense of being singled out, and there’s definite room for growth in our policies and responses.

After taking in the new input, my stance is still leaning toward YTA, but I’m more conflicted than before. I fully acknowledge what others are saying about the necessity of respecting staff religious boundaries and clearly outlining shop policies—those aspects really aren’t about personal discrimination, and I see how a visible, consistently-applied policy can actually be a form of respect and transparency. But the repeat concern among multiple folks about rigid policies harming folks on the margins really sticks with me; the intent behind the rule isn’t malicious, but the real-world effect on someone requesting a basic, routine men’s cut—who just happens to be a woman or isn’t strictly cis male—can leave them feeling singled out or unworthy of service, even if unintentionally. What I take most seriously from the exchange is that following policy by the letter isn’t always sufficient, especially in these awkward gray-zone moments; genuine attempts at bridges, flexible creativity, or more empathetic language can sometimes do as much good as strict adherence to rules. At the same time, I now better understand the challenges shops face in trying to be both fair and culturally/religiously sensitive—expecting perfection feels unrealistic. So overall, my updated view is: you weren’t malicious or trying to discriminate, and the shop was reasonably transparent about the rule, but the way it played out still inadvertently created a negative experience and left someone feeling excluded because of a gendered policy. For me, that tips lightly toward YTA—not egregiously so, but enough to warrant re-thinking these kinds of policies and focusing more on building flexibility and care into shop practices moving forward.

Reading everyone’s latest takes has made me reflect even more on where I stand. I’m still of the mind that, as the barber, following the clearly posted policy—one set for sincerely held religious boundaries, training realities, and transparent customer expectations—means you weren’t acting maliciously or with intent to discriminate. But after hearing repeated points about the real impact on those who don’t fit easily into typical gender categories, I recognize now that maintaining a firm men/women policy, even with clear reasons, really does risk alienating or hurting certain customers, especially when a simple men’s cut (well within the barber’s usual scope) is all that’s asked. I don’t think the refusal, under the existing rules, constitutes being an “asshole,” so I still lean NTA in this exact scenario—but I have to admit, following the letter of the policy may be causing more discomfort than intended.
